title: Stale but Stable: Staleness-Adaptive Trust Regions for Stabilizing Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
why: If you run async RL to keep GPUs busy, this paper offers a drop-in change to the PPO clip rule that holds AIME24 accuracy roughly flat from lag 1 to lag 8 on a 30B MoE model, instead of degrading as rollouts go stale.
notes: The diagnosis: PPO clipping only gates sampled outward updates, so it is a sampled surrogate rather than a full-policy trust region; under staleness from policy lag, engine delays, and MoE routing drift, high-mismatch updates go weakly controlled.

SAT uses the detached sampled log-ratio as a staleness proxy, applies staleness-based kernel scaling to find high-mismatch tails within each batch, and contracts only the sign-selected endpoint of the nominal PPO interval, so ordinary tokens keep baseline behavior.
Theory offered: local interval containment and pointwise pessimism relative to PPO, i.e. SAT's interval sits inside PPO's and never gives a less conservative update.

Setup is a decoupled asynchronous RL stack on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base, SGLang for inference and Megatron for training. Reported AIME24 avg@8: SAT-GSPO with routing replay (R3) at 35.83 (lag 1) and 34.79 (lag 8); SAT-GSPO alone at 34.17 (lag 1).

Adaptive clipping and routing replay are framed as complementary: one targets mismatch tails, the other MoE routing inconsistency. Caveat: results are single-model, single-benchmark, and avg@8 gaps of about one point on AIME24 are within the range where seed variance matters; the abstract reports no variance or baseline-at-lag-8 numbers.
summary: The paper argues that in asynchronous RL, where rollout generation is decoupled from optimization, PPO's clipping fails as a trust region because it only constrains sampled outward updates while training-inference divergence drives approximation error. The proposed Staleness-Adaptive Trust Region (SAT) treats the detached sampled log-ratio as a staleness proxy, uses staleness-based kernel scaling to identify high-mismatch tails within a batch, and contracts only the sign-selected endpoint of the PPO clip interval for those tokens. The authors prove local interval containment and pointwise pessimism versus PPO, characterizing how the rule reshapes update geometry under heterogeneous staleness. Experiments use a decoupled async setup on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base with SGLang inference and Megatron training; SAT-GSPO with routing replay (R3) reports the best AIME24 avg@8 at 35.83 (lag 1) and 34.79 (lag 8), and SAT-GSPO alone reaches 34.17 at lag 1. Adaptive clipping and routing replay are presented as complementary stabilizers for mismatch tails and MoE routing inconsistency. Evidence is limited to one model and one math benchmark, with no variance figures in the abstract.
novelty: adaptive PPO clip intervals tuned to per-token staleness in async RL
audience: RL researchers/engineers building large-scale async LLM RL training pipelines

title: LG to ban residential proxies from smart TV apps
why: Nearly half of LG's TV app catalog was quietly reselling household bandwidth as proxy exit nodes, meaning traffic attributed to a home IP may originate from a Pac-Man clone on the living room screen, and platform-level suspension is now the only control users have.
notes: Spur's measurement: more than 42 percent of apps in LG's webOS store and more than 25 percent of Samsung Tizen apps ship residential proxy SDKs, monetizing the owner's bandwidth indefinitely.
Bright Data supplied the majority of proxy SDKs across both TV platforms and did not respond to Krebs' requests for comment.

LG's remedy is enforcement by removal: SVP John Taylor says developers must strip the proxy option or have their apps suspended, with the review "well underway." No timeline, app counts, or audit method disclosed.

Proxy vendors named in the report claim KYC vetting (customers largely doing content scraping) and technical controls blocking access to other devices on the host LAN; those are vendor assertions, unverified in the article.

Spur's Trevor Sutter frames the problem as consent theater on devices consumers cannot audit: a one-time in-app prompt, sometimes accepted by a minor in the household, is not ongoing control or platform oversight.
Unrelated but in the same piece: Gamers Nexus showed certain LG LCD monitors auto-install a McAfee antivirus upsell app delivered through Windows Update with no approval prompt.
summary: LG Electronics USA told KrebsOnSecurity it will suspend webOS smart TV apps that do not remove residential proxy SDKs, which turn a television into an always-on proxy node rented to third parties. The commitment follows research by the security firm Spur, covered July 2, that found more than 42 percent of apps in LG's webOS store and more than a quarter of apps for Samsung's Tizen OS bundled such SDKs, in everything from Pac-Man-style games to screensavers and file utilities. Bright Data accounted for a majority of the proxy SDKs across both platforms and did not respond to requests for comment; the named proxy providers say they run know-your-customer checks, tied largely to content scraping, and use countermeasures to keep customers from reaching other devices on the host's local network. LG SVP John Taylor said a residential proxy network is not an intended use of LG smart TVs, that the app review is "well underway," and that LG will strengthen evaluation of developer-submitted apps. Spur's Trevor Sutter argues the core issue is scale plus auditability: a buried one-time consent prompt is not meaningful transparency, especially when the person clicking through may be a minor in the household. The piece also notes Gamers Nexus reporting that certain LG LCD monitors auto-install an app promoting paid McAfee subscriptions, delivered via Windows Update with no approval prompt.
novelty: LG commits to suspending apps with residential proxy SDKs
audience: security researchers and privacy-conscious consumers

title: DataFlow-Harness: A Grounded Code-Agent Platform for Constructing Editable LLM Data Pipelines
why: If you are wiring coding agents into data infrastructure, this paper argues the output format is the lever: making the agent mutate a live DAG through an MCP-exposed operator registry cut reported cost 72.5% and latency 49.9% against Vanilla Claude Code while leaving an artifact humans can keep editing.
notes: The framing: coding agents emit scripts that vanish into a file rather than persistent, editable platform objects. The authors call this the NL2Pipeline gap and close it by restricting the agent to typed, incremental mutations on a platform-native DAG.

Three components: DataFlow-Skills (procedural guidance), an MCP layer that hands the agent the live operator registry and current pipeline state, and DataFlow-WebUI, which synchronizes chat-based authoring with a visual DAG editor.
Reported results on a 12-task data-engineering benchmark: 93.3% observed end-to-end pass rate; 72.5% lower monetary cost and 49.9% lower generation latency versus Vanilla Claude Code.
Against a stronger Context-Aware Claude Code baseline, the pass rate is 0.9 percentage points lower while cost is 42.8% lower, so the pitch is cost parity-plus, not accuracy superiority.
Per-task analysis says Skills pay off mainly where pipeline construction depends on implicit procedural knowledge, implying limited gain on tasks fully specified by the operator registry.
Caveats: 12 tasks is a small benchmark, results are author-reported, and the abstract omits benchmark provenance, underlying model versions, run variance, and how pass/fail was judged.
summary: DataFlow-Harness is a research platform that constrains an LLM coding agent to build data pipelines as platform-native directed acyclic graphs via typed, incremental mutations, instead of emitting free-form scripts. The authors name the underlying problem the "NL2Pipeline gap": agent-generated scripts are not materialized as persistent, editable platform artifacts. The system has three parts: DataFlow-Skills for procedural guidance, a Model Context Protocol layer that exposes the live operator registry and current pipeline state to the agent, and DataFlow-WebUI, which keeps conversational authoring in sync with a visual DAG editor. On a 12-task data-engineering benchmark, the authors report a 93.3% observed end-to-end pass rate, with 72.5% lower measured monetary cost and 49.9% lower generation latency than Vanilla Claude Code, and a pass rate within 0.9 percentage points of a Context-Aware Claude Code baseline at 42.8% lower cost. Per-task analysis attributes most of the Skills benefit to tasks requiring implicit procedural knowledge. The abstract does not describe benchmark construction, task difficulty, model versions, or run counts, so the numbers are self-reported and unverified.
novelty: agents build editable DAG pipelines, not throwaway scripts
audience: engineers building LLM-driven data-engineering/agentic pipeline tools

title: Gemini last models: temperature, top_p, and top_k are deprecated and ignored
why: If your Gemini calls set temperature, top_p, or top_k, or prefill a model turn to force JSON, those knobs are now ignored and will return HTTP 400 on future model generations: control moves to system instructions, structured outputs, and a `thinking_level` enum.
notes: Sampling control is gone: Google says `temperature`, `top_p`, and `top_k` are deprecated and silently ignored starting with Gemini 3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash-Lite, and will error in future generations. The recommended substitute for determinism is a system instruction with explicit rules, which is not an equivalent mechanism and the docs offer no evidence on how well it substitutes.

Prefilled model turns now fail: a request whose last non-empty turn has role `model` returns HTTP 400. Google points users to `system_instruction` or Structured outputs, and to server-side `previous_interaction_id` for multi-turn state instead of client-assembled histories.

Pricing and specs: Gemini 3.6 Flash is $1.50/1M input and $7.50/1M output (down from $9.00/1M output on 3.5 Flash), default thinking level `medium`; Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite is $0.30/1M input and $2.50/1M output, default `minimal`. Both carry a 1M-token context window, 64k max output, and Computer Use as a native tool.

The only numbers given are vendor-reported and for Flash-Lite against Gemini 2.5 Flash: HLE 18.0% vs 11.0%, CharXIV 74.5% vs 63.7%. No methodology, and the 3.6 Flash claims (fewer turns and tool calls, less loop spiraling, better code) are qualitative with no benchmarks attached.

Migration also drops `candidate_count` (unsupported in 3.x) and replaces `thinking_budget` with the string enum `thinking_level` ("minimal"/"medium"/"high"). Google concedes a regression: human evaluators preferred earlier models for visual layout and styling, and 3.6 Flash's preference for running diagnostic scripts first adds exploratory steps on simple frontend work.
Gemini 3.6 Flash is now the default model behind the Antigravity agent in Gemini Managed Agents (`antigravity-preview-05-2026`), overridable via an API field.
summary: Google's migration guide announces GA for Gemini 3.6 Flash ($1.50/1M input, $7.50/1M output, default thinking level `medium`) and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite ($0.30/1M input, $2.50/1M output, default `minimal`), both with 1M-token context, 64k max output, thinking, and native Computer Use. The structurally important change is to the API surface: `temperature`, `top_p`, and `top_k` are deprecated and ignored for these and all future Gemini models, with an HTTP 400 promised in later generations, and requests ending in a `model` role turn (prefill) now return 400 immediately. Google directs developers to system instructions, Structured outputs, and server-side `previous_interaction_id` in the Interactions API in place of those techniques; `thinking_budget` becomes the enum `thinking_level`, and `candidate_count` is unsupported in 3.x. Self-reported gains for Flash-Lite over Gemini 2.5 Flash are cited as HLE 18.0% vs 11.0% and CharXIV 74.5% vs 63.7%, without methodology; claims for 3.6 Flash (fewer reasoning steps and tool calls, less execution-loop spiraling, better instruction following) are qualitative. Google notes two regressions: human evaluators preferred earlier models on visual layout and styling, and 3.6 Flash's tendency toward upfront diagnostic scripts adds steps on simple frontend tasks. Gemini 3.6 Flash also becomes the default model for the Antigravity agent in Gemini Managed Agents.
novelty: Gemini 3.6 Flash/3.5 Flash-Lite drop sampling params, add Interactions API
audience: developers building on Gemini API who need to migrate model configs

title: NexForge: Scaling Executable Agent Tasks via Requirement-First Synthesis
why: If the results hold, a 35B open-weight model trained on synthesized tasks reaches 75.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, which means agent capability is now gated by data-generation pipelines rather than access to curated repos or tool graphs.
notes: The stated bottleneck is substrate-first synthesis: tying task generation to predefined tools, repos, or skill graphs means coverage grows only by manual substrate expansion, each domain needs a bespoke pipeline, and task distributions track substrate convenience instead of real demand.

NexForge's pipeline: research-based demand discovery (task forms, scenarios, relative prevalence), distribution-aware task compilation, automatic retrieval or construction of files, repos, dependencies and runtime configs, then teacher rollout collection and trajectory distillation.

Reported numbers: 3,600 terminal and 2,000 office tasks from the same pipeline lift Qwen3.5-35B-A3B Base from 22.5% to 52.0% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and 813 to 1338 Elo on GDPval; 43.2K terminal tasks reach 58.4%, which the authors say surpasses Claude Opus 4.6.

The Nex-N2 model family, trained partly on NexForge data, is reported at 75.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 1585 Elo on GDPval, claimed as state-of-the-art open source and ahead of several proprietary frontier systems. Weights are said to be publicly available.

Caveats from the abstract alone: all figures are self-reported by the authors, the teacher model used for rollouts is unnamed, there is no ablation separating demand discovery from sheer task volume, and cross-benchmark comparisons span Terminal-Bench 2.0 and 2.1.
summary: NexForge is a framework for generating executable agent training data starting from free-form capability requirements rather than from an existing substrate of tools, repositories, or skill graphs. It runs research-based demand discovery to estimate representative task forms and their prevalence, compiles tasks to match that distribution, automatically assembles the files, repositories, dependencies and runtime configurations each task needs, and then collects teacher rollouts for trajectory distillation. The authors report that one pipeline, with no domain-specific infrastructure, produced 3,600 terminal tasks and 2,000 office tasks, raising Qwen3.5-35B-A3B Base from 22.5% to 52.0% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and from 813 to 1338 Elo on GDPval; scaling to 43.2K terminal tasks reached 58.4%, which they say exceeds Claude Opus 4.6. Data from the pipeline also feeds Nex-N2, a publicly released agent model family reported at 75.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 1585 Elo on GDPval and claimed as state-of-the-art open source. The abstract does not describe ablations, the teacher model, or contamination controls, so the comparisons remain author-reported.
novelty: requirement-first (not tool-first) synthesis of agent training tasks
audience: researchers/engineers building agent training pipelines and benchmarks

title: Ask Twice, Look Twice: Prompt Echoing Resolves the Question-First Paradox in Vision-Language Models
why: A prompt-only edit, restating the question before and after the image, recovers up to 19 Winoground group-accuracy points on open VLMs with no training, fine-tuning, or architecture change.
notes: The claimed 'question-first paradox': putting the question before the image underperforms the image-first ordering recommended for frontier VLMs across VQA benchmarks, at a cost of up to 17.5 group-accuracy points across five open VLMs.

Diagnosis via logit-lens and attention probes: a question placed before the image does steer perception (image patch representations move toward question-relevant concepts), but stranded behind hundreds of image tokens it is barely attended by the answer token, which commits to image-driven, often wrong answers.

A causal attention knockout is offered as evidence that the answer token reads the question only when the question follows the image, isolating a downstream readout failure from the upstream perception effect.

The fix, 'question echoing': restate the question on both sides of the image so one copy steers perception and the other is read out at answer time; echoing the image as well is claimed to restore the whole-image view a causal decoder otherwise loses.

Reported results: echoed prompts surpass the best single-pass ordering on NaturalBench, POPE, Winoground, and open-ended VQAv2, by up to 19 Winoground group-accuracy points, with no training or architecture change.

Framed as a parallel to a fifty-year-old human 'adjunct questions' finding: repeating a question before and after a passage aids comprehension more than either position alone; all numbers are self-reported and limited to five open-weight VLMs.
summary: The paper reports a "question-first paradox" in vision-language models: placing the question before the image underperforms the image-first ordering recommended for frontier VLMs across visual question answering benchmarks, costing up to 17.5 group-accuracy points across five open VLMs. Using logit-lens and attention probes, the authors argue the question-before-image position genuinely steers perception toward question-relevant concepts, but the question, stranded behind hundreds of image tokens, is barely attended by the answer token; a causal attention knockout indicates the answer reads the question only when it follows the image. Their training-free fix, "question echoing," restates the question on both sides of the image so one copy steers perception and the other is read at answer time, and echoing the image too is said to restore a whole-image view the causal decoder loses. Echoed prompts are reported to beat the best single-pass ordering on NaturalBench, POPE, Winoground, and open-ended VQAv2, by up to 19 Winoground group-accuracy points, with no training, fine-tuning, or architecture change. The authors draw an analogy to a fifty-year-old psychology result on human "adjunct questions." All figures are self-reported and confined to open-weight VLMs.
novelty: training-free prompt-echoing fix for VLM question placement
audience: engineers building VLM/VQA pipelines and prompt engineers optimizing multimodal inference

title: China's 'open' AI is a terrible business, and nothing like open-source software
why: The labs behind the open-weight models you deploy (GLM, Kimi, MiniMax) are losing 3-5x their revenue and rationing compute, so the frontier weights you download come from businesses whose survival depends on subsidy, not economics.
notes: Zhipu (Z.ai), maker of GLM 5.2, lost about $500M on roughly $107M revenue last year per its public filings; its stock fell more than 40% in the month after GLM 5.2's launch.
MiniMax lost $250M on $79M revenue; shares dropped more than 50% in a month. Both are among the few publicly traded independent Chinese labs.

Moonshot AI halted new signups for its Kimi K3 open-weight model days after launch, citing insufficient compute, illustrating that each new user raises the infra bill rather than being near-free like software distribution.

The article's core argument: open weights are not open source. There is no Red Hat support/services upsell; revenue comes from selling inference, and inference flows to the most efficient operator, usually cloud giants (Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Oracle, Alibaba), not the model creator. Alibaba stock rose ~13% in the same month as an inference host.

Framed as strategy: analysts (William Blair's Arjun Bhatia, Barclays' Raimo Lenshow) argue Chinese labs release with 'little regard for near-term profitability' to commoditize AI and force OpenAI/Anthropic to cut prices; Xi Jinping publicly endorsed 'open-source, openness, collaboration, and sharing' in a Shanghai speech, adding state pressure to keep giving models away.
Caveat: the analysis rests on two publicly traded labs plus analyst notes; the loss figures are self-reported filings and the strategic-intent framing is attributed opinion, not disclosed policy.
summary: Business Insider argues that China's acclaimed open-weight AI labs are poor businesses because open weights differ economically from open-source software: software copies cost nearly nothing to distribute, but each additional model answer requires paid chips, power, and datacenter capacity. Financials cited from public filings show Zhipu (Z.ai) losing about $500M on ~$107M revenue and MiniMax losing $250M on $79M, with both stocks falling 40-50% in a month despite the launch of GLM 5.2 and industry praise; Moonshot AI halted Kimi K3 signups for lack of compute. Analysts (William Blair's Bhatia, Barclays' Lenshow) note there is no Red Hat-style services upsell, and inference revenue flows to whoever operates infrastructure most efficiently, typically cloud giants like Alibaba (up ~13%) rather than the model maker. The piece frames the giveaway as a challenger strategy to commoditize AI and pressure US closed-model firms' margins, reinforced by Xi Jinping's public call for openness, which pushes Chinese labs to keep releasing weights even at the cost of profitability. The loss numbers are self-reported and the strategic-intent reading is analyst opinion rather than stated policy.
novelty: financial data showing Chinese open-weight labs bleeding cash despite acclaim
audience: investors and engineers evaluating open-weight AI business models

title: China is considering export controls on AI technologies, including banning local companies from using TSMC, report claims — restrictions would also cover advanced AI models, training data, and overseas acquisitions
why: If Beijing follows through, the open-weight edge that DeepSeek and Moonshot give downstream builders could be walled off, and Chinese fabless designers like Alibaba and Huawei would lose access to TSMC's leading-edge nodes.
notes: Per a Financial Times report citing two people familiar with the talks, China's Ministry of Commerce has consulted Alibaba, ByteDance, and Zhipu about restricting foreign downloads of model weights and limiting transfers of AI training data abroad; overseas customers could still access Chinese models remotely via API.

A separate proposal under consultation would bar Chinese chip designers (Alibaba, ByteDance, Huawei named) from fabbing advanced processors at TSMC or other foreign fabs, funneling orders to SMIC despite SMIC trailing TSMC on process technology.

DeepSeek and Moonshot currently ship downloadable open-weight models that users can self-host and modify, contrasted against closed flagship models from Anthropic and OpenAI; download restrictions would erase that distribution advantage.
New foreign-acquisition controls are aimed partly at closing the loophole that let Meta buy Manus for $2 billion, a deal Beijing subsequently ordered unwound; agentic AI firms are called out.

The measures would be folded into China's export-restricted technology catalogue, which already lists rare-earth materials, their processing methods, and several lithium-ion battery production technologies.

All proposals remain at the industry-consultation stage and are not finalized; the article notes such controls would also slow global adoption of Chinese AI standards, weakening China's position abroad.
summary: The Financial Times, citing two people familiar with the talks, reports that China's Ministry of Commerce is weighing an expansion of export controls covering advanced AI models, training data, and foreign acquisitions of strategic tech firms. Regulators have consulted Alibaba, ByteDance, and Zhipu about restricting foreign users from downloading model weights and limiting cross-border transfers of training data, though remote API access to Chinese models would remain. A more contentious proposal would prevent Chinese designers such as Alibaba, ByteDance, and Huawei from manufacturing advanced chips at TSMC and other foreign fabs, directing that work to SMIC. Separate acquisition rules target agentic AI companies and aim to close the loophole behind Meta's $2 billion Manus purchase, which Beijing later forced to unwind. The measures could enter China's export-restricted technology catalogue, which already lists rare earths and lithium-ion battery tech. Download curbs would blunt the open-weight edge that DeepSeek and Moonshot hold over closed models from Anthropic and OpenAI; all proposals remain under industry consultation and are not finalized.
novelty: China may restrict open-weight model downloads and TSMC fabbing of Chinese chip designs
audience: AI policy watchers, semiconductor/geopolitics analysts

title: Masked Diffusion Language Models are Strong and Steerable Text-Based World Models for Agentic RL
why: If the claims hold, you can generate diverse agent-RL training environments with a masked diffusion model that beats autoregressive LLMs 4x its size, cutting the cost of building specialized RL simulators.
notes: The core argument: autoregressive world models have a left-to-right bias that blocks conditioning on globally interdependent anchors (tool schemas, prior turns, expected outcomes); masked diffusion LMs (MDLMs) use bidirectional anchor-aware denoising to condition on all of them at once.

Training data: 239,403 grounded state-action trajectories curated across nine open-source environments and twelve frontier model families; task is formalized as steerable transition dynamics decomposed into initial state, task context, tool schemas, domain rules, and steering directives.
Self-reported result: MDLMs beat AR LLMs over 4x their parameter size on coherence, groundedness, and rollout diversity at comparable inference latency.

Zero-shot transfer on three OOD environments (ScienceWorld, ALFWorld, AppWorld) across 1.2B-7B agent backbones (LFM2.5, Qwen3, Mistral) claims up to 47% absolute gains over baselines without environment-specific fine-tuning.

Ships a plug-and-play GRPO training framework with deterministic state checks; adds adversarial failure-mode analysis and human evaluation on realism, outcome correctness, and training utility; code and data open-sourced.
Caveat: numbers are the authors' own; the abstract does not name the baselines beaten or give absolute scores, and 'up to 47%' is a ceiling, not a mean.
summary: This arXiv paper argues that masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) make better text-based world models for agentic reinforcement learning than autoregressive LLMs, because bidirectional denoising can condition on globally interdependent state anchors (tool schemas, prior turns, expected outcomes) that left-to-right generation cannot. The authors formalize text world modeling as a steerable transition-dynamics problem and curate 239,403 grounded state-action trajectories from nine open-source environments and twelve frontier model families. They report that MDLMs outperform AR LLMs more than 4x their size on coherence, groundedness, and empirically measured rollout diversity at comparable inference latency, and introduce a plug-and-play GRPO training framework with deterministic state checks. Zero-shot transfer tests on three out-of-distribution environments (ScienceWorld, ALFWorld, AppWorld) with 1.2B-7B backbones (LFM2.5, Qwen3, Mistral) claim up to 47% absolute gains over baselines without environment-specific fine-tuning. The work includes adversarial failure-mode analysis and human evaluation, and the code and data are open-sourced. All performance figures are self-reported and the abstract does not specify baselines or absolute numbers.
novelty: masked diffusion beats larger AR LLMs as world models for agent RL
audience: RL/agent researchers building synthetic training environments for LLM agents

title: AI Didn't Make Programming Easier. It Just Made It Differently Difficult
why: The cognitive bottleneck of your job is moving from recall to judgment: the skill that now separates good developers is evaluating whether AI-generated code is correct and maintainable, not remembering syntax.
notes: Frames AI coding assistants as external memory that offloads syntax recall, boilerplate, and API lookup, shifting scarce working memory toward architectural reasoning, impact analysis, and validation; the authors argue debugging, refactoring, and systems analysis still require internal mental models the AI cannot supply.

Grounds the argument in prior cognitive-science work: Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory model, Pennington's mental-model research, and Siegmund et al.'s fMRI finding that code comprehension activates working-memory, attention, and language networks.

Cites Barke, James, and Polikarpova that developers use Copilot to offload low-level work while shifting effort to validating and integrating generated code, framed as evidence the tool is an integrated cognitive extension rather than a faster search engine.

Reports mixed learning evidence: Shihab et al. found students finished brownfield tasks faster with Copilot but reported not understanding why suggestions worked; Alanazi et al.'s meta-analysis found AI improves task performance but yields only small, statistically unstable gains in learning and comprehension.

Names four claimed shifts: lower entry barrier to producing code (but a higher bar for producing good code), work that is differently difficult rather than easier, education bending from syntax memorization toward systems thinking, and the programmer's role moving from knowledge vessel to orchestrating agent.

This is a CACM opinion essay applying frameworks (distributed cognition, cognitive load theory, Extended Mind Hypothesis); it synthesizes existing studies rather than presenting new experiments or measurements.
summary: A CACM opinion essay argues that AI coding assistants do not make programming easier but relocate its cognitive load, acting as external memory that absorbs syntax recall, boilerplate, and API lookup while raising the burden of evaluating, integrating, and validating generated code. Drawing on cognitive-science work (Baddeley and Hitch, Pennington, Siegmund et al.'s fMRI study) and frameworks like distributed cognition, cognitive load theory, and the Extended Mind Hypothesis, the authors treat the model as an integrated part of the programmer's cognitive architecture rather than a search engine. They cite empirical findings that developers offload low-level work to Copilot (Barke et al.) and that students complete tasks faster but understand suggestions less well, with meta-analysis showing only small, unstable learning gains (Shihab et al.; Alanazi et al.). The core claim is that the hard part moves from recall ("how do I write this?") to judgment ("does this make sense?"), so debugging, refactoring, and architectural reasoning still depend on internal mental models. The essay predicts four shifts: lower entry barriers alongside a higher bar for good code, differently-difficult work, education pivoting toward systems thinking, and the programmer becoming an orchestrating agent. It is a synthesis of prior research, not new experimental evidence.
novelty: reframes AI coding tools via cognitive science, not productivity hype
audience: software engineers and CS educators rethinking skill development in AI-assisted coding

title: My USB Drive Has a Hidden Encrypted Vault
why: A working open-source hardware design shows how to hide an AES-256 vault behind an 8GB decoy volume that no OS can see, aimed at threat models where you can be compelled to decrypt.
notes: Built on WCH's CH569 (same maker as the CH340 USB-serial chip), using its USB3, SD/eMMC interface, and hardware AES block; an SM4 block also exists but is unused. SD card replaces eMMC because AI demand has inflated eMMC prices.

The device enumerates as an 8GB drive with no OS-visible way to detect the hidden partition; writing the literal string 'password:PASSWORD' into a plaintext file on the disk triggers unmount and remount of the encrypted section, decrypting in place.

It is not filesystem-aware: firmware snoops raw WRITE10 buffers for the 'password:' prefix, copies the password to RAM, and zeroes the buffer so it is never written to disk. Side effect: any user data containing 'password:' can cause an accidental match.

KDF is 100,000 rounds of SHA-256 over password plus a per-device salt derived from the USB serial ID (ID_SERIAL_SHORT), tuned to a ~3s unlock and a stated 5s ceiling; author says Argon2 is off the table because it is memory-hard and the chip is at its compute limit.

Self-reported throughput: ~9MB/s write and 20MB/s read with AES-CTR, ~6MB/s write and 10MB/s read with AES-XTS. Author defaults to CTR despite its documented counter-reuse risk, judging XTS's gain not worth the speed hit.

Case is epoxy-glued so tampering requires destroying the device; encryption is verified only against OpenSSL's AES via functional tests. A wave of AI-generated GitHub issues (mostly hallucinated or already-patched) triggered a Reddit dogpile, but one real AES-XTS problem surfaced. A preorder page is live.
summary: Phantomdrive is an open-source (firmware, hardware, mechanical) USB drive that appears as a plain 8GB stick but hides a second AES-256-encrypted partition the OS cannot detect. Unlocking works by writing the string 'password:PASSWORD' into a plaintext file; firmware snoops raw USB WRITE10 commands for the 'password:' prefix, extracts the key material to RAM, zeroes the buffer, then remounts the hidden section. It runs on WCH's CH569 using USB3, an SD card (chosen over pricey eMMC), and a hardware AES block, with the case epoxy-glued to force physical destruction on tamper attempts. The KDF is 100,000 rounds of SHA-256 over the password plus a per-device salt taken from the USB serial ID, tuned to keep unlock under ~5 seconds; the author notes Argon2 is infeasible because the chip lacks memory-hard capacity. Encryption is verified only via functional tests against OpenSSL, and the author defaults to AES-CTR (~9MB/s write, 20MB/s read) over AES-XTS despite acknowledging CTR's counter-reuse risk. The write-up also recounts a wave of AI-generated GitHub issues, mostly hallucinated but one legitimate AES-XTS concern, that sparked a Reddit dogpile; a preorder page is live.
novelty: open-source USB stick with hidden AES-256 vault triggered by password file
audience: hardware/security engineers interested in DIY encrypted storage and crypto design tradeoffs

summary: As web-scraped data increasingly contains AI-generated text that risks model collapse, ISBNdb is selling bulk acquisition of pre-2022 printed books to AI labs, pitching them as curated, edited human knowledge that is "structurally clean" of AI contamination and author poisoning. It brokers orders of 1,000 to 1 million books, offers strict NDAs to hide client identity, and openly acknowledges the bad optics of destroying books to scan them. The practice traces to Anthropic internal documents (surfaced in a January copyright suit) detailing plans to buy, scan, and destroy millions of books via marketplaces like Better World Books, with contractor Datamation offering destructive scanning; Google faces a separate suit over Gemini training. Judge William Alsup ruled Anthropic's copies fair use precisely because the print originals were destroyed and not shared externally, a legal argument ISBNdb now advertises. title: Apple Defeats Liability for Not Scanning iCloud for CSAM
why: A federal court just confirmed that Section 230 shields cloud providers from CSAM design-defect liability even when internal messages show they knew their service was used for it, so any duty to scan encrypted storage now has to come from Congress, not litigation.
notes: Amy v. Apple Inc., 2026 WL 2031817 (N.D. Cal. July 13, 2026): the court dismissed the third amended complaint, which alleged Apple's refusal to deploy any known CSAM detection was a design defect.

Section 230 immunity was held to apply because the claims treat Apple as a publisher and because avoiding liability would require Apple to act as a publisher; the opinion states scienter is irrelevant, so alleged internal knowledge (per Apple text messages) does not defeat immunity.

Plaintiffs' attempts to route around 230 via Doe v. Twitter (reporting-infrastructure defect), Lemmon v. Snap (provider-created content), and Roommates.com (modifying content) were all rejected; the court distinguished a duty to fix reporting systems from a duty to deploy scanning tools like NeuralHash or PhotoDNA.
Apple built its own NeuralHash rather than adopting PhotoDNA, then abandoned scanning and shipped end-to-end encryption for iCloud files; the case teed up for a Ninth Circuit appeal on 230 scope.

Judge Wise ruled for Apple but wrote that no law requires or forbids proactive CSAM detection and urged lawmakers to mandate it, acknowledging any mandate would cost 'at least some loss of privacy for millions.'

Blogger Eric Goldman argues the ruling downplays encryption, that forced scanning breaks end-to-end encryption for everyone, and that government prosecution, not weakening encryption, should be the primary anti-CSAM tool.
summary: A Northern District of California court dismissed Amy v. Apple, a putative class action alleging Apple's failure to deploy any known CSAM detection in iCloud was a design defect. The court held Section 230 grants Apple complete immunity because the claims treat Apple as a publisher of third-party content and because escaping liability would require Apple to act as a publisher; alleged internal knowledge that iCloud was used to share CSAM does not matter because scienter is irrelevant to 230. Plaintiffs' attempts to use the Doe v. Twitter, Lemmon v. Snap, and Roommates.com exceptions all failed. Apple had built NeuralHash instead of adopting PhotoDNA, then abandoned scanning and implemented end-to-end encryption for iCloud. Judge Wise ruled for Apple but wrote pointedly that current law neither requires nor prevents proactive CSAM detection and called on lawmakers to legislate a mandate, noting it would come at a privacy cost. Blogger Eric Goldman, summarizing the opinion, argues it understates the encryption stakes and that breaking end-to-end encryption should not be a regulatory option; the case is positioned for a Ninth Circuit appeal.
novelty: court dismisses CSAM design-defect suit against Apple, urges Congress to act
audience: tech lawyers, platform policy/trust-and-safety engineers, privacy advocates

title: ICE to Pay Thomson Reuters $125 Million to Find ‘Voter Fraud’
why: A federal agency is committing $125M to continuously monitor millions of people using commercial data that includes SSNs, credit-header records, geolocation, and license-plate reads, with "voter fraud" named as a stated target for the first time.

title: Claude Is Not a Compiler
why: A working engineer describes shipping a geo-distributed, consistent DNS server in about a week of attention while reading almost none of the code, and stays able to answer every design question his team asks afterward.
notes: The core argument: the 'coding agent as compiler' framing is wrong because LLMs work vertically across strategy, product, architecture, code, and machine code, whereas a compiler only handles source-to-binary. The author calls this 'vibe-engineering' (guiding decisions at every layer) versus 'vibe-coding' (handing off a task and letting the agent decide).

Concrete case: exe.dev VMs get vm-name.exe.xyz domains; VMs boot faster than DNS could propagate, so they built a custom DNS server. Adding regions made single-region (Oregon) DNS the latency bottleneck and deploys caused small outages, motivating a geographically distributed, fully consistent DNS server.

Workflow: humans set high-level strategy in person (general-purpose server with tweaks, hub-and-spoke, append-only replication, persistence at edges), then multiple concurrent agent loops built full implementations with tests and adversarial review; new agents did differential analysis comparing implementations to surface decisions the agents made silently and differently.

Design detail: replication catches up via 'entries since row N' plus long-poll; database rollbacks break the append-only contract, solved by a randomly-generated 'timeline' field per row so a mismatch on sync triggers a full clean re-sync. Author repeated the throw-one-away differential process three times total.

Self-reported outcome: final system had unit tests, end-to-end tests, a shadow mode for prod rollout, and agent-authored docs; zero DNS incidents a month after launch. Author claims he understands the system well enough to reason about it and guide future agent work despite not reading most code. Numbers and results are the author's own, no external verification.

Framing caveats the author keeps: agents can't yet match an experienced dedicated human on individual tasks, and lower layers aren't fully relinquished, citing that a few Go stdlib routines are hand-written assembly where you can't trust the compiler.
summary: In this follow-up to 'Is Claude a Compiler?', the author argues the compiler analogy is a category error: unlike a compiler that only translates source to binary, an LLM works vertically across strategy, product, architecture, code, and machine code without meetings or permission. He distinguishes 'vibe-coding' (handing off a task to an agent that makes the decisions) from 'vibe-engineering' (using agents to accelerate a human's decisions at every layer, including which decisions matter). The load-bearing example is exe.dev building a geographically distributed, consistent DNS server after their single-region self-built server became a latency and uptime bottleneck; LLMs researched designs, taught DNS internals and security history, evaluated alternatives like AXFR/IXFR, and multiple concurrent agents produced implementations with tests and adversarial review that were then compared for divergences. A notable design choice is a per-row randomly-generated 'timeline' field to detect database rollbacks that violate the append-only contract, forcing a full re-sync on mismatch. The author reports the effort took about a week of his attention, that he read very little of the code yet can reason about and answer questions on the system, and that there were zero DNS incidents a month post-launch (all self-reported). He concludes that some abstraction layers that provide only convenience are dying, but layers that encode important decisions comprehensibly will persist, and that vibe-engineering is becoming just engineering.
novelty: LLMs work vertically across abstraction layers, not just as a code-compiling layer
audience: engineers using AI coding agents on systems-level infrastructure work

title: How to pack ternary numbers in 8-bit bytes
why: The exact trick behind llama.cpp's ternary weight types: 5 trits per byte at 1.6 bits/trit, decoded in SIMD without a single division, which is what makes BitNet b1.58 and TriLM inference fast on AVX2 and NEON.
notes: A ternary digit (trit) has 3 states; log2(3) = 1.585 bits is the theoretical floor. Packing 5 trits per 8-bit byte uses 243 of 256 possible states, hitting 1.6 bits/trit, or 99.06% of ideal density. Other block sizes are worse: 3 trits/5 bits gives 1.667, 4 trits gives 1.75.

Packing treats the 5 trits as a base-3 number, then converts to a fixed-point fraction below 1 via b = ((b*256) + 242) // 243. The ceiling division cancels the off-by-one truncation error introduced during later digit extraction.

Unpacking avoids modulo and division entirely: multiply the byte by 3, take the top bits (b >> 8) as the most-significant trit, mask the low byte (b & 0xFF), repeat 5 times. SIMD lacks integer modulo/divide, so this multiply-and-shift approach is the point.
Asymmetry is deliberate: packing (which uses division) happens once when storing LLM weights; unpacking happens on every inference pass and is division-free.
Correctness was checked exhaustively in C over all 243 valid byte values, comparing modulo-based base-3 digits against the fixed-point extraction; all PASS.
Merged into llama.cpp as the ternary types for TriLMs and BitNet b1.58 via PR #8151, with both AVX2 and ARM NEON implementations.
summary: The post explains how llama.cpp packs ternary (-1, 0, 1) weights for BitNet b1.58 and TriLM models at 1.6 bits per trit by fitting 5 trits into one byte, using 243 of 256 states for 99.06% of the log2(3) theoretical density. Packing encodes the five trits as a base-3 number and converts it to a fixed-point fraction with the expression ((b*256)+242)//243, where the ceiling division corrects an off-by-one truncation error. Unpacking then extracts each trit by repeatedly multiplying by 3 and reading the top bits, avoiding the integer modulo and division operations that SIMD does not support. The scheme is asymmetric by design: packing runs once when weights are stored and may use division, while the frequent unpacking path stays division-free for speed. The author verifies losslessness with an exhaustive C test over all 243 valid byte values, and the technique is merged in llama.cpp PR #8151 with AVX2 and ARM NEON implementations.
novelty: SIMD-friendly ternary weight packing at 1.6 bits/trit, no modulo needed

title: Python 3.15's Ultra-Low Overhead Interpreter Profiling Mode – Ken Jin's Blog
why: CPython 3.15's JIT records execution traces at roughly 4.5x interpreter overhead on a toy benchmark by swapping dispatch tables instead of branching or duplicating the interpreter, so JIT profiling stops being the thing that eats the JIT's gains.
notes: The trick: keep two dispatch tables (normal and tracing) and switch modes by assigning a local variable (DISPATCH_TABLE_VAR), so no per-instruction branch and no doubled binary. The macros ENTER_TRACING/LEAVE_TRACING just point the variable at TRACING_DISPATCH_TABLE or DISPATCH_TABLE.

The tracing table is a fan-in/fan-out design: every opcode maps to one profiling/recording instruction that does the profiling work, then dispatches through the fixed normal table to the real next instruction. Entering and leaving profiling is just initializing/finalizing data structures plus swapping tables.

Reported overhead on the author's toy benchmark (median of 40 runs, dynamic frequency scaling off): 1.72e-06s interpreter-only vs 7.47e-06s with profiling plus JIT compilation, about 4.5x. Compared against PyPy's 900x-1000x meta-tracing slowdown, which the author notes is not a fair comparison since PyPy traces the interpreter itself.

The earlier approach, a separate profiling interpreter called into from the normal one, was fine for the tail-calling interpreter but caused roughly a 6% pyperformance slowdown on the computed-goto interpreter, attributed to effectively doubling the C interpreter's size (computed goto is function-scoped). A boolean 'profile' flag was rejected as too disruptive despite good branch prediction.

Benchmarking used PYTHON_JIT_RESUME_INITIAL_VALUE=1 to force JIT compilation; the test calls a function containing many repeated 'x + x' statements. Author is a CPython core developer and says the technique is undocumented elsewhere as far as he could find.

Author's own caveat: the system is elegant but hard to reason about, and he questions whether the complexity is worth it; he frames the technique as reusable for low-overhead interpreter profiling or runtime type profiling, not just trace recording.
summary: Ken Jin, a CPython core developer, describes the low-overhead interpreter profiling behind CPython 3.15's JIT trace recording. Rather than calling into a separate profiling interpreter (which bloated the computed-goto binary and cost ~6% on pyperformance) or gating profiling on a boolean flag (rejected as too disruptive), the implementation keeps two dispatch tables and swaps them by setting a local variable, avoiding branches and code duplication. The tracing table maps all opcodes to a single recording instruction that performs profiling and then fans out through the normal fixed table to execute the real next instruction. On a toy benchmark of median 40 runs, profiling plus JIT compilation ran about 4.5x slower than the bare interpreter (7.47e-06s vs 1.72e-06s), which the author contrasts with PyPy's 900x-1000x meta-tracing overhead while acknowledging that is not a like-for-like comparison. He presents the technique as undocumented, reusable beyond trace recording, and elegant but complex enough that he questions whether it is worth the maintenance burden.
novelty: dispatch-table swapping enables near-zero-overhead JIT tracing in CPython 3.15
audience: systems/language-runtime engineers and CPython internals followers

title: Self-State Attacks on Self-Hosted AI Agents: How Far Can OS Defenses Go?
why: If you run agents that read and write their own memory and config, some corruption attacks look identical to normal file activity at the OS layer, so OS access controls and syscall monitoring alone cannot catch them.
notes: Threat model: an agent is subverted by corrupting its own state files (memory, config, instructions) through legitimate OS system calls, so the malicious actions are indistinguishable from ordinary agent I/O at the syscall level.

summary: The paper defines "self-state attacks," a threat class in which a self-hosted AI agent is compromised through corruption of its own memory and configuration files using legitimate OS system calls rather than external exploits. The authors characterize the attack space along four axes (Target, Mechanism, Granularity, Temporal) and instantiate it as a 23-cell matrix comprising 43 concrete operations on real self-state files, injected into live activity traces collected from a representative self-hosted agent run under distinct workload profiles. They evaluate canonical and workload-conditioned defenses, and report that a layered stack (access-control prevention on instruction and configuration layers, workload-conditioned anomaly detection on the memory layer, periodic backup for recovery) is effective across most attack cells. A small residual attack surface remains structurally indistinguishable from legitimate behavior at the OS level, which the authors argue can't be closed by OS-level defenses alone. The paper is a framework and empirical study; numbers are self-reported by the authors, and the trace set comes from a single representative agent.
novelty: formalizes "self-state attacks" where agents corrupt own memory/config via legit syscalls

title: DeepSearch-World: Self-Distillation for Deep Search Agents in a Verifiable Environment

summary: DeepSearch-World is a deterministic, verifiable web-agent environment with reproducible search and page-reading tools and 420K multi-hop QA tasks generated from entity-level random walks. On top of it, DeepSearch-Evolve runs a self-distillation loop that alternates trajectory generation, filtering, data mixing, and fine-tuning, without pulling supervision from any stronger teacher model. The authors motivate this against supervised fine-tuning on fixed teacher trajectories and sparse-reward RL, both of which supervise long-horizon tool use poorly.
